source.author: lucan
source.text: Bella per Emathios plus quam civilia campos Iusque datum sceleri canimus, populumque potentem In sua victrici conversum viscera dextra, Cognatasque acies, et rupto foedere regni, Certatum totis concussi viribus orbis In commune nefas, infestisque obvia signis Signa, pares aquilas, et pila minantia pilis.
source.text_original: Bella per Emathios plus quam civilia campos / Iusque datum sceleri canimus, populumque potentem / In sua victrici conversum viscera dextra, / Cognatasque acies, et rupto foedere regni, / Certatum totis concussi viribus orbis / In commune nefas, infestisque obvia signis / Signa, pares aquilas, et pila minantia pilis.
source.text_english: Wars worse than civil through the Emathian plains, and law given to crime, we sing, and a mighty people turned upon its own entrails with victorious hand, and kin-born battle lines, and, with the bond of sovereignty broken, conflict with the whole strength of the shaken world for a common wickedness, standards meeting hostile standards, equal eagles, and javelins threatening javelins.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Prima deum magnis canimus freta pervia natis fatidicamque ratem, Scythici quae Phasidis oras ausa sequi mediosque inter iuga concita cursus rumpere flammifero tandem consedit Olympo.
reuse.text_original: Prima deum magnis canimus freta pervia natis / fatidicamque ratem, Scythici quae Phasidis oras / ausa sequi mediosque inter iuga concita cursus / rumpere flammifero tandem consedit Olympo.
reuse.text_english: First we sing of the sea passages made traversable by the great sons of the gods, and of the prophetic ship, which, daring to follow the Scythian shores of Phasis and, driven on, to break through its course amid the middle mountain ridges, at last settled on fiery Olympus.
